title: Kafka Connect & Schemas: The Field Handbook
summary: A dense, practical guide to Kafka Connect — source and sink connectors, the converter layer, Schema Registry, and compatibility rules — covering internals, configuration, trade-offs, and the mistakes that break pipelines in production.

chapters.title: Why Kafka Connect Exists
points: Definition: Kafka Connect is a framework + runtime for streaming data between Kafka and external systems without writing producer/consumer code.
Problem it solves: every team writing its own bespoke ingest/egress app duplicates retry, offset, scaling, and schema logic.
Source connector = external system → Kafka topic. Sink connector = Kafka topic → external system.
Connect is a data-movement layer, not a transformation engine — heavy joins/aggregations belong in Kafka Streams or ksqlDB.
Config-driven: a connector is created by POSTing JSON to the REST API, not by deploying code.
Runs as a cluster of workers (JVM processes); connectors and tasks are distributed across them.
Standalone mode: single process, offsets in a local file — good for demos, CDC of a local file, edge collection. No fault tolerance.
Distributed mode: multiple workers sharing a `group.id`, state in internal Kafka topics — the production default.
Three internal topics: `config.storage.topic` (compacted, 1 partition), `offset.storage.topic` (compacted, ~25 partitions), `status.storage.topic` (compacted, ~5 partitions).
Replication factor of internal topics must be ≥3 in production; the default of 1 is a common data-loss footgun.
Connect gives at-least-once delivery by default; exactly-once for source connectors requires `exactly.once.source.support=enabled` (Kafka 3.3+).
Plugin model: connectors are JARs on `plugin.path`, isolated by classloader so two connectors can use conflicting library versions.
Confluent Hub / Maven are the common distribution channels; `connect-plugin-path` conflicts are the #1 startup failure.
Comparison: Connect vs custom app — Connect wins on ops (offset management, restart, scaling); custom app wins on arbitrary business logic.
Mental model to keep for the whole handbook: `external system ⇄ connector ⇄ SMT ⇄ converter ⇄ Kafka bytes`.

chapters.title: Connect Runtime Internals: Workers, Connectors, Tasks
points: Worker: a JVM process that hosts connector and task instances and exposes the REST API on port 8083.
Connector instance: the *coordinator* — it does no data copying; it computes the list of task configs.
Task: the unit that actually moves data. `tasks.max` caps how many the connector may create.
`tasks.max` is a ceiling, not a guarantee — a JDBC source with 3 tables creates at most 3 tasks regardless of `tasks.max=10`.
Source task loop: `poll()` returns `List<SourceRecord>`; the framework produces them and periodically commits source offsets.
Sink task loop: `put(Collection<SinkRecord>)` receives batches; `flush()`/`preCommit()` marks Kafka consumer offsets as committed.
Sink connectors are just consumer groups — group name is `connect-<connector-name>`; you can inspect lag with `kafka-consumer-groups`.
Source offsets are connector-defined maps (e.g. `{"table":"orders","incrementing":4711}`) stored in the offset topic, keyed by source partition.
Rebalancing: adding/removing a worker triggers redistribution of tasks. Incremental cooperative rebalancing (default since 2.3) avoids stop-the-world.
`connect.protocol=sessioned|compatible|eager` controls the rebalance protocol; `eager` is the old stop-the-world behavior.

REST endpoints to memorize: `GET /connectors`, `POST /connectors`, `PUT /connectors/{n}/config`, `GET /connectors/{n}/status`, `POST /connectors/{n}/restart?includeTasks=true`, `DELETE /connectors/{n}`.
A connector can be RUNNING while its tasks are FAILED — always check task status, not just connector status.
Restarting a *connector* does not restart failed *tasks* unless `includeTasks=true` is passed.
Worker configs (`bootstrap.servers`, converters, `plugin.path`) are process-level; connector configs are per-connector and override converters.
Trade-off: more tasks = more parallelism but more connections to the source DB — a JDBC source with 50 tasks can exhaust the DB connection pool.

chapters.title: Source Connectors in Practice
points: Source connector responsibilities: discover work units, poll for new data, emit `SourceRecord` with key, value, schemas, and source offset.
JDBC source modes: `bulk` (re-read everything each poll), `incrementing` (monotonic ID column), `timestamp`, `timestamp+incrementing` (safest of the query modes).
`incrementing` mode misses updates and deletes — it only sees new rows with a higher ID.
`timestamp` mode misses rows committed with an earlier timestamp than one already read (the transaction-clock skew problem); `timestamp.delay.interval.ms` mitigates it.
Log-based CDC (Debezium) reads the DB transaction log (MySQL binlog, Postgres WAL, Oracle LogMiner) — captures inserts, updates, AND deletes with full before/after images.

Comparison — query-based JDBC vs log-based CDC: JDBC is simple + no DB privileges, but polls, misses deletes, and loads the DB. CDC is low-latency, complete, but needs replication privileges and careful slot/binlog retention.
Debezium envelope shape: `{before, after, source, op, ts_ms}` where `op` ∈ `c` (create), `u` (update), `d` (delete), `r` (read/snapshot).
Tombstones: for a delete, Debezium emits the change event plus a null-value record on the same key so log compaction removes it.
Snapshotting: initial consistent read of existing rows, then switch to streaming. `snapshot.mode=initial|never|schema_only|when_needed`.
Postgres replication slots hold WAL until consumed — a stopped Debezium connector can fill the disk on the primary. Monitor `pg_replication_slots`.
Topic naming: source connectors usually emit `<prefix><table>`; `topic.prefix` is mandatory in modern Debezium.
Record key choice: use the primary key so compaction and downstream upserts work; a null key gives round-robin partitioning and destroys per-entity ordering.
Ordering guarantee is per-partition only — a table streamed to a multi-partition topic keyed by PK preserves per-row order, not global order.
Example config skeleton: `connector.class`, `tasks.max`, `database.hostname`, `topic.prefix`, `table.include.list`, `key.converter`, `value.converter`.
Gotcha: changing `name` of a connector resets its source offsets — Connect keys offsets by connector name, so the rename causes a full re-snapshot.

chapters.title: Sink Connectors in Practice
points: Sink connector consumes from one or more topics (`topics` list or `topics.regex`) and writes into an external store.
Delivery semantics: at-least-once by default — the external system must tolerate duplicates, ideally via idempotent upserts on a key.
`insert.mode=insert|upsert|update` in the JDBC sink; `upsert` plus `pk.mode=record_key` is the standard idempotent pattern.
`pk.mode`: `none`, `kafka` (topic/partition/offset as PK), `record_key`, `record_value`.
Auto-DDL: `auto.create=true` creates the target table from the record schema; `auto.evolve=true` issues `ALTER TABLE ADD COLUMN` on schema growth.
Auto-evolve can only ADD nullable columns — it never drops, renames, or narrows types. Plan migrations for anything else.
Batching: `batch.size` / `consumer.max.poll.records` control throughput; too large a batch risks exceeding `max.poll.interval.ms` and triggering a rebalance.
S3 sink partitioners: `DefaultPartitioner`, `FieldPartitioner`, `TimeBasedPartitioner` (with `path.format`, `partition.duration.ms`, `timezone`).
S3/HDFS sinks commit files on `flush.size` or `rotate.interval.ms` — small `flush.size` produces the small-files problem downstream.
Elasticsearch sink: `write.method=upsert`, document ID from the record key; `behavior.on.null.values=ignore|delete|fail` decides tombstone handling.
Dead letter queue: `errors.tolerance=all`, `errors.deadletterqueue.topic.name=dlq-x`, `errors.deadletterqueue.context.headers.enable=true` to keep the failure cause in headers.
`errors.tolerance=none` (default) means one poison record kills the task — good for correctness, bad for availability. Pick deliberately.
`errors.retry.timeout` and `errors.retry.delay.max.ms` give bounded retries before the DLQ path.
Consumer overrides use the `consumer.override.` prefix (e.g. `consumer.override.auto.offset.reset=earliest`); requires `connector.client.config.override.policy=All` on the worker.
Gotcha: deleting and recreating a sink connector with the same name keeps the consumer group and its offsets — it resumes, it does not replay.

chapters.title: Converters: The Bytes Boundary
points: Converter = the pluggable component that translates between Connect's internal `SchemaAndValue` and the raw bytes on the wire.
Direction matters: source = Connect data → bytes (serialize); sink = bytes → Connect data (deserialize). Same class, both ways.
Connect's internal data model is schema-aware: `Schema` (type, name, optional, default, version) + `Struct` for records.
Connect logical types: `Decimal`, `Date`, `Time`, `Timestamp` — annotated primitives carrying a logical name.
`key.converter` and `value.converter` are set independently; a very common pairing is `StringConverter` for the key and Avro for the value.
`StringConverter`: bytes ⇄ UTF-8 string, no schema. Fine for keys, lossy for structured values.
`ByteArrayConverter`: pass-through, no interpretation — used for opaque blobs and binary passthrough pipelines.
`JsonConverter` with `schemas.enable=true` embeds the schema in EVERY message: `{"schema":{...},"payload":{...}}` — self-describing but hugely bloated.
`JsonConverter` with `schemas.enable=false` emits plain JSON; sinks then receive schemaless `Map`s, and many sinks (JDBC) reject that.
`AvroConverter`, `ProtobufConverter`, `JsonSchemaConverter` all register schemas with Schema Registry and write a compact payload + schema ID.
Wire format for registry-backed converters: `[magic byte 0x00][4-byte big-endian schema ID][payload]` — 5 bytes of overhead per record.
Converter configs are namespaced: `value.converter.schema.registry.url`, `value.converter.schemas.enable`, `value.converter.enhanced.avro.schema.support`.
Worker-level converters are defaults; connector-level converter settings override them per connector.
Classic error `Unknown magic byte!` = a non-Avro message (often plain JSON or a String key) read by an Avro converter.

Comparison table: JSON+schema (readable, ~3-5× larger, no central governance) vs Avro (compact, evolvable, needs registry) vs Protobuf (compact, great cross-language codegen) vs JSON Schema (readable + governed, middle ground).
Rule: converters are a topic-level contract — every producer and consumer of a topic must agree, not just Connect.

chapters.title: Schema Registry: Mechanics
points: Schema Registry is a REST service storing versioned schemas and handing out globally unique integer schema IDs.
Its own storage is a compacted Kafka topic, `_schemas` — the registry is stateless and rebuilds from that log on restart.
Subject = the namespaced scope under which schema versions are registered and compatibility is checked.
`TopicNameStrategy` (default): subjects are `<topic>-key` and `<topic>-value`.
`RecordNameStrategy`: subject is the record's fully-qualified name — lets one topic carry multiple event types with independent evolution.
`TopicRecordNameStrategy`: `<topic>-<record.name>` — per-topic *and* per-type, the usual pick for event-type unions on one topic.
Producer path: serializer looks up (subject, schema) in a local cache; on miss it POSTs to register, gets an ID, and prepends it to the payload.
Consumer path: deserializer reads the 5-byte prefix, fetches the writer schema by ID (cached), and decodes against the reader schema.
Avro's superpower: reader and writer schemas can differ; Avro resolves them field-by-field using names and defaults.
Key REST calls: `GET /subjects`, `GET /subjects/{s}/versions`, `GET /schemas/ids/{id}`, `POST /subjects/{s}/versions` (register), `POST /subjects/{s}/versions/{v}` (check-if-exists).
Compatibility endpoints: `GET/PUT /config` (global) and `GET/PUT /config/{subject}` (per-subject override).
Dry-run before deploy: `POST /compatibility/subjects/{s}/versions/latest` returns `{"is_compatible": true|false}` without registering.
`auto.register.schemas=true` is convenient in dev and dangerous in prod — a buggy service can register a bad schema. Set false and register via CI.
`use.latest.version=true` plus auto-register false makes producers use the registered schema rather than their compiled-in one.
Deletes: soft delete (`DELETE /subjects/{s}`) hides the subject; hard delete (`?permanent=true`) frees the version number and can strand consumers.
Registry outage behavior: cached schemas keep working; NEW schema IDs cannot be resolved, so unseen-schema consumption stalls. Cache size matters.

chapters.title: Compatibility Rules & Schema Evolution
points: Compatibility answers one question: can code holding schema version A safely process data written with version B?
`BACKWARD` (default): new schema can read data written by the previous schema. Consumers upgrade first.
`BACKWARD_TRANSITIVE`: new schema can read data written by ALL previous versions — required when old data stays on the topic forever.
`FORWARD`: previous schema can read data written by the new schema. Producers upgrade first.
`FORWARD_TRANSITIVE`: all previous schemas can read the new one.
`FULL`: both backward and forward against the immediately previous version. `FULL_TRANSITIVE`: both, against all versions.
`NONE`: no checks. Use only for throwaway topics; it disables the one guardrail you have.
BACKWARD-allowed changes: DELETE a field, ADD a field WITH a default.
FORWARD-allowed changes: ADD a field, DELETE a field that HAS a default.
FULL-allowed changes: add or remove ONLY optional fields that have defaults.
Never allowed under any non-NONE mode: renaming a field without an alias, changing a field's type incompatibly (e.g. `string` → `int`), removing an enum symbol under forward compat.
Field renames are safe only via Avro `aliases` — the reader maps the old name onto the new one.
Type promotion Avro permits: `int → long → float → double`, and `string ⇄ bytes`. Narrowing is never safe.
Adding a value to an enum breaks forward compatibility unless the enum declares a `default` symbol (Avro 1.9+).
Union evolution: `["null","string"]` with default `null` is the idiomatic optional field — a bare `"string"` field with no default can never be removed backward-compatibly.
Choose per data lifetime: infinite-retention/compacted topics → `*_TRANSITIVE`; short-retention event streams → plain `BACKWARD` is usually enough.

chapters.title: Single Message Transforms & Predicates
points: SMTs run per-record, in-process, between the connector and the converter — no external system, no state, no joins.
Order matters: source = connector → SMT chain → converter. Sink = converter → SMT chain → connector.
Chain syntax: `transforms=a,b` then `transforms.a.type=...`, `transforms.a.<option>=...` for each named step.
`InsertField` — add a static value, topic, partition, offset, or timestamp as a field.
`ExtractField$Key` / `$Value` — pull one field out and make it the whole key or value; the standard way to key a CDC stream by its PK.
`ValueToKey` — copy fields from the value into a Struct key; usually paired with `ExtractField$Key`.
`Cast`, `ReplaceField` (include/exclude/rename), `MaskField` (redact PII), `TimestampConverter` (string ⇄ epoch ⇄ Date).
`RegexRouter` — rewrite the destination topic name with `regex` + `replacement`; the usual prefix-stripping tool.
`Flatten` — collapse nested Structs into `parent.child` columns so a JDBC sink can write them.
`ExtractNewRecordState` (Debezium) — unwrap the CDC envelope down to the `after` image, with `delete.handling.mode` and `add.fields` options.
Predicates gate an SMT: `predicates=isDead`, `predicates.isDead.type=...RecordIsTombstone`, then `transforms.x.predicate=isDead`.
Built-in predicates: `TopicNameMatches`, `HasHeaderKey`, `RecordIsTombstone`. `negate=true` inverts them.
SMTs modify the schema too — the transformed schema is what gets registered, so an SMT change can trip compatibility checks.
Cost: each SMT is a per-record allocation; long chains measurably reduce throughput. Prefer Kafka Streams past ~5 transforms.
Hard limits: no aggregation, no joining across records, no external lookups, no splitting one record into many.

chapters.title: Failure Modes, Ops & Common Mistakes
points: Mistake: internal topics with replication factor 1 — a single broker loss loses all connector configs and offsets.
Mistake: `schemas.enable=true` on JsonConverter in high-volume pipelines — 3-5× storage and network for no governance benefit.
Mistake: mismatched converters between producer and Connect sink — surfaces as `Unknown magic byte!` or a JSON parse error, not as a schema error.
Mistake: setting `tasks.max` high and expecting parallelism the connector cannot provide (single-table JDBC, single-binlog Debezium = always 1 task).
Mistake: no DLQ, `errors.tolerance=none`, and one malformed record halting the whole pipeline at 3am.
Mistake: DLQ configured but never monitored — data silently disappears into it for weeks.
Mistake: renaming a connector, or changing `topic.prefix`/`database.server.name`, and unintentionally triggering a full re-snapshot.
Mistake: `auto.register.schemas=true` in production, letting a rogue deploy register an incompatible schema under the wrong subject.
Mistake: hard-deleting a schema version that in-flight consumers still need to resolve by ID.
Mistake: assuming Connect gives exactly-once — it does not, unless source EOS is explicitly enabled and the sink is idempotent.
Sink lag diagnosis: `kafka-consumer-groups --describe --group connect-<name>` shows real lag; the Connect status API does not.
Metrics to alarm on: `connector-task-metrics.status`, `sink-record-lag-max`, `source-record-poll-rate`, `deadletterqueue-produce-requests`, rebalance rate.
Recovery order: read `GET /connectors/{n}/status` → find the failed task's trace → fix the config or the poison record → `POST /restart?includeTasks=true`.
Offset surgery: modern Connect exposes `GET/PATCH/DELETE /connectors/{n}/offsets` (connector must be STOPPED) — replaces the old hand-editing of the offsets topic.
Capacity rule of thumb: size workers by heap and network, not CPU; sinks that batch to object storage need heap proportional to `flush.size` × record size.
Security: propagate credentials via `config.providers` (e.g. `FileConfigProvider`, Vault) so secrets never sit in plaintext in the config topic.

chapters.title: Design Decisions & Recap
points: Format decision: Avro if you are JVM-heavy and want compact evolvable records; Protobuf if you need polyglot codegen and gRPC alignment; JSON Schema if humans read the topic; plain JSON only for low-volume or legacy interop.
Ingest decision: log-based CDC when you need deletes, low latency, or no DB load; query-based JDBC when you lack replication privileges or the table is append-only.
Compatibility decision: `BACKWARD` for short-lived event streams, `FULL_TRANSITIVE` for compacted state topics and long-retention data lakes.
Subject strategy decision: `TopicNameStrategy` for one type per topic; `TopicRecordNameStrategy` for an event-type union that must stay ordered on one topic.
Transform decision: SMT for field-level shaping; Kafka Streams / Flink when you need joins, aggregation, or one-to-many fan-out.
Deployment decision: standalone only for edge/dev; distributed with ≥3 workers and RF=3 internal topics everywhere else.
Trade-off — throughput vs latency: larger batches and longer `flush.interval` raise throughput and cut per-record cost, at the price of end-to-end delay and bigger replay windows.
Trade-off — availability vs correctness: `errors.tolerance=all` keeps the pipeline up but accepts silent data loss into the DLQ; `none` guarantees you notice.
Trade-off — governance vs velocity: `auto.register.schemas=false` + CI registration slows teams down and prevents the outages that slow them down more.
Cost model: registry-backed formats add ~5 bytes/record and one cached HTTP lookup per new schema ID — negligible next to embedded-schema JSON.
Rollout recipe for a breaking change: create a v2 topic, dual-write from the source, migrate consumers, verify lag and counts, then retire v1. Never mutate a schema past its compatibility mode.

Pre-deploy checklist: converters agreed, compatibility mode set per subject, `tasks.max` matched to real parallelism, DLQ topic created and monitored, internal topics RF=3, secrets via config providers.
One-line recap of the pipeline: `source system → connector → SMTs → converter → Schema Registry ID + bytes → Kafka → bytes + ID → converter → SMTs → connector → sink system`.
Three rules to leave with: the converter is a topic-wide contract; compatibility mode must match data lifetime; every offset is keyed by connector name, so names are permanent.
Next steps: read the Debezium connector docs for your database, run `kafka-avro-console-consumer` to inspect real payloads, and script compatibility checks into CI.
